# Module 3: Discipline Equals Freedom

Module 3 argues that a performance department's meeting problems are really meeting-type problems: people arrive expecting different outcomes, the room drifts, and time disappears. The fix is discipline written down. Name the modality of every meeting (Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build), time-box it, pre-read where possible, and capture every output in a decision log with an owner, action, due date, and review. The Kaigi decision meeting and the Stoplight Storytelling one-slide brief are the two operational tools; the meeting typology cheat sheet and the Lab 3D worksheet make the system teachable to staff. The webinar and podcast supply the argument underneath: a leader's executive function is a finite resource, ambiguity and coordination burn it, and the only way to buy back time for strategy and deep work is to make routine operations predictable through common language, defined channels, documented procedures, strategic intent with clear decision boundaries, and direct feedback.

## Lessons

### Lab 3A: Kaigi Meeting Structure (video 13:37; Lab_3a_Blog_Kaigi_agendas.pdf, 3 pp.)

- Kaigi (Japanese for a meeting; used here to mean a decision meeting) is built for speed, clarity, and accountability. It is not for debate, ideation, or education (transcript 01:24 to 02:18; blog p.1).
- It only works when the question is clear, the options are limited (usually 2 to 3), information can be pre-read, and the team needs alignment fast. Six options is not options, it is uncertainty, and that belongs in Diagnose (blog p.1).
- Time-box contributions. 120 seconds is a typical limit; pre-training environments can run at 30 seconds per point. If a point cannot land quickly, it is not ready and goes offline (blog p.2; transcript 03:43 to 04:48).
- Every Kaigi ends with a decision log entry: owner, action, due date, review process, recorded as an audit trail. "Kaigi without a decision log is just a fast meeting that creates slow confusion later" (blog p.2).
- Two use cases: the pre-training go/no-go and a late-meeting mode switch when a Diagnose meeting stalls (blog p.2; transcript 07:28 to 13:23).
- The speaker admits the decision log is admin he did poorly early in his career, and suggests rotating an "on audit" staff member to keep the log as a development task (transcript 04:48 to 05:56).

### Lab 3B: Meeting Typology (video 08:12; Lab_3b_Blog_Meeting_typology.pdf, 3 pp.; Lab_3b_Meeting_Typology_Cheat_Sheet.pdf, 2 pp.)

- Four modalities: Decide (commit to action), Diagnose (understand a known problem, test hypotheses), Inform (broadcast updates and context), Build (co-create and design). Name the modality up front and the meeting becomes easier to run (blog p.1; cheat sheet p.1).
- Diagnose is the classic 30-minute multidisciplinary meeting where the problem is known but the solution is not. Controls: agree the problems in advance, allocate time per item, and do not pretend to have information you lack. Pattern: Diagnose, assign a small group to gather what is missing, return inside a defined window, then Kaigi to decide (blog pp.1 to 2).
- Inform meetings turn into accidental problem-solving when a key stakeholder is not across the detail and the group re-explains in real time. Keep catch-ups targeted: one meeting, one stakeholder, one or two core staff (blog p.2).
- Ops and stand-ups should feel Kaigi-like: what is happening, what is blocked, who owns it, what is next (blog p.2).
- Build meetings need more space and less pressure, but often must finish with a Decide step or they produce ideas, not outcomes (blog p.2).
- After Action Reviews and Postmortems are learning engines only if blameless: timelines, facts, metrics, honesty about what could not be measured, learning as the goal rather than "accountability theatre" (blog p.2).
- One staff meeting can carry several modalities in sequence (inform, diagnose, three Kaigi items) as long as each segment is named (transcript 04:03 to 04:37; cheat sheet p.1 "don't mix modes without saying so").

### Lab 3C: Stoplight Storytelling (video 08:07; Lab_3c_Blog_Stoplight_storytelling.pdf, 2 pp.; Lab_3c_Stoplight_Storytelling_Slide_Template.pdf, 3 pp.)

- Most debate in performance environments is caused by unclear briefs, not disagreement. Fix how people present before demanding speed (blog p.1).
- Stoplight Storytelling is a one-slide decision brief with a Green (continue), Amber (hold, monitor, review soon), Red (stop or change now) status, designed to sit inside Kaigi-style meetings (blog p.1).
- Six-part anatomy: headline question, stoplight status, one chart maximum, signal versus noise shown against SEM and MDC, one ask written as a verb, accountability (owner, action, due date, review date) logged (blog p.1).
- If the change does not exceed system noise, do not dress it up as insight. Convergent evidence is allowed but capped at two bullets (blog p.2).
- Charts fail when pretty but unreadable: axes labelled, differences labelled, clear at a glance, no dual axes or decoding puzzles. "Clarity beats sophistication in decision meetings" (blog p.2; transcript 04:25 to 05:51).
- Nothing hangs. Even Amber needs what is monitored, who owns it, and when it is reviewed (for example 48 hours). Two minutes is the benchmark; if it needs explaining, it is the wrong meeting type (blog p.2; template p.2).

### Lab 3D: Meetings as an Educational Tool (video 09:06; Lab_3D_Blog_Meetings_as_an_education_tool.pdf, 2 pp.; Lab_3D_Worksheet.pdf, 3 pp.)

- Meetings are a repeatable, observable opportunity for staff to practise preparation, clarity, decision discipline, and follow-up. Give staff meetings to run rather than only mentoring them (blog p.1).
- Guardrails create freedom: define what the meeting is for, the agenda, duration, required outputs, and how actions are tracked. Leadership sets the six-lane highway (strategy); staff choose when to change lanes (tactics); nobody drives off-road (blog p.1).
- Do not protect quiet staff from meetings. Scaffold: simple meeting, one topic, one slide, one time box, debrief, repeat. "Confidence doesn't arrive first. Repetition arrives first" (blog pp.1 to 2).
- The speaker tracked who spoke and who did not, called on the quiet ones with advance notice, and gave his head physiotherapist ownership of the medical review meeting (transcript 01:46 to 03:56).
- For young practitioners: ask your boss for the smallest meeting you can run; leadership skills are practised, not taught (blog p.2).
- A CEO habit: pose the problem, then sit quietly until someone starts. Assign a staff member to argue the opposite with data so the leader can test their own bias before deciding (blog p.2; transcript 06:14 to 08:49).

### Webinar 3: Discipline Equals Freedom, Parts I to III (three videos, 11:43, 10:27, 11:28; no PDF)

- Part I: executive function is limited; every decision, ambiguity, and coordination task depletes it. The same question ("talk to me about training load") from a head coach, a physician, and an Athletic Performance coach is three different questions requiring three different translations. When systems are predictable, routine operations become automatic and the prefrontal cortex is freed for strategy, innovation, and pattern recognition (Part I 00:59 to 04:08).
- Part I: the paradox of discipline (attributed to Jocko Willink; the transcript renders it "Willnick"): rigid fundamentals create room to adapt under pressure. A coach who demanded "nimble" got it only because he was the most disciplined planner the speaker ever worked with. "Avoiding structure to stay flexible actually makes you reactive" (Part I 05:05 to 11:30). A 10-person team has 45 connection possibilities, so coordination overhead scales fast (Part I 10:03 to 10:31).
- Part II: five practices: develop a common language, create communication mechanisms, build an operational procedures list, lead by strategic intent, provide clear and honest feedback (Part II 00:39 to 01:09).
- Part II: common language means demystify. Report in the coach's verbal anchors (jog, stride, sprint, "gut run"), not metres per second. Give coaches a cheat sheet before the season, never introduce a new variable mid-season, and listen to how a coach communicates and mirror it (tables if they want tables) (Part II 02:08 to 06:11).
- Part II: communication mechanisms: define which channel carries what, agree the injury-communication tempo with the head coach in advance (safe first, best estimate after the post-game talk, physician update after next-morning scans), tag messages urgent / routine / FYI, put objective, duration, and required prep on every meeting invite, and set response-time expectations (Part II 06:11 to 10:09).
- Part III: operational procedures put repeatable tasks (equipment, session prep, data collection, testing) on autopilot so the leader works on the business, not in it. Documented procedures travel with you between jobs: "build it once and sell it 15 times" (Part III 00:00 to 03:56).
- Part III: lead by strategic intent. Strategy is the six-lane highway, tactics is the car changing lanes. A first-year hire gets one or two lanes; a ten-year colleague gets all six. Staff must know what they can decide and what to push up the chain (Part III 03:56 to 06:30).
- Part III: feedback on a structured cycle (monthly, half-year), do not let small things fester, document consequential conversations, and ask for feedback on yourself (Part III 07:18 to 09:15).

### Podcast 3: 20 Minutes of Discipline (audio 16:59; no PDF)

- Attention drops after 15 to 20 minutes, and Parkinson's law means a 60-minute slot fills with fluff when 20 minutes of work exists. Context switching between poorly structured meetings drains the analytic capacity that moves the needle (02:58 to 04:24).
- Example: a five-person planning meeting run with a stopwatch, three questions, 60 seconds to think and 120 seconds to answer each, done in about 40 minutes, set up three months of work (01:28 to 02:58).
- Amazon's narrative memos are cited, but the speaker prefers sending pre-read 24 hours ahead and requiring it to be read (04:33 to 05:24; 07:46 to 08:11).
- Protect the windows between training, gym, and treatment for cognitive work; the speaker now hard-blocks weekly project time for staff and asks them to share the output back (05:24 to 07:20).
- Simple structure: state the required outcome first, focus on what is working, what is not, and what must change, name an arbiter if a decision is needed, end with actions, deadlines, and who reports back (07:20 to 09:39).
- Add-ons: parking lot with a dedicated process (subject, who, action), 15-minute agile stand-ups (what did I do, what will I do, what is blocking me), Google's 50/25-minute buffers, Shopify's meeting cost calculator, Bezos's two-pizza teams for multidisciplinary sub-groups (10:50 to 14:10).
- Objections answered: "too complex for 20 minutes" means the pre-work is not done, so break it into smaller pieces; brainstorming is generative work, not decision-making; relationship-building belongs at coffee or lunch, not in operational meetings (12:16 to 15:13).

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. The four modalities (cheat sheet p.1; 3A blog p.1; 3B blog p.1)

Every meeting has one primary job. Name it at the top of the invite.

| Modality | Job |
| --- | --- |
| Decide | Commit to an option and assign ownership |
| Diagnose | Understand a known problem; test hypotheses |
| Inform | Distribute updates and shared context |
| Build | Co-create or design a new workflow, system, or solution |

The cheat sheet p.2 and 3B blog p.2 add "Learn" as a label for After Action Reviews and Postmortems, which are run as Diagnose/Build. Treat it as four modalities plus a Learn application.

### 2. Universal rules for every meeting (cheat sheet p.1)

1. Name the modality at the top of the invite: Decide / Diagnose / Inform / Build.
2. Time-box every agenda item (tempo protects clarity).
3. Pre-read where possible (especially for Decide).
4. One meeting = one primary job (do not mix modes without saying so).
5. Capture outputs immediately (log decisions; list actions).

Minimum decision-log fields: Decision / Ask (verb), Owner, Action, Due date, Review date, Notes (data, SEM/MDC if relevant).

### 3. Meeting typology table (cheat sheet p.2, reproduced in full; source wording kept)

| Meeting type | Modality | Typical time box | Best for | Required outputs | When to avoid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kaigi (Decision Meeting) | Decide | 15 to 30 min (or shorter) | Clear question + 2 to 3 options + alignment fast | Decision log: owner, action, due date, review | Vague question, missing info, ideation, teaching |
| Pre-training Kaigi (Go/No-go) | Decide | 5 to 12 min | Rapid readiness decisions | Decision log + immediate comms | Deep debate, complex new analysis, long explanations |
| Stoplight Storytelling (tool inside Kaigi) | Decide support | 2 min per slide | Quick decision briefs (Green/Amber/Red) | One ask (verb), one chart max, owner/action/due/review | Multiple asks, multiple charts, new complex info |
| Problem-solving / Case meeting | Diagnose | ~30 min | Known problem, solution unclear; multidisciplinary hypotheses | Actions list: info needed, who gathers, by when | When you need a decision now (switch to Kaigi) |
| Info Broadcast / Update | Inform | 10 to 30 min | Admin updates, shared context, alignment on facts | Notes + any follow-ups | If it turns into problem solving or decision debate |
| Ops / Stand-up (Inform + Unblock) | Inform + micro-Decide | 10 to 15 min | Status, blockers, quick assignments | Owner + next step (micro log or action list) | Deep diagnosis, design work, long round-robin updates |
| Design / Co-creation session | Build | 45 to 90 min | New workflow/system, structure changes, creation | Draft artifact + next steps; often ends with Kaigi | When you need fast operational decisions |
| After Action Review (AAR) | Learn (Diagnose/Build) | 15 to 30 min | What happened? What did we learn? (blameless) | Learning points + procedure changes + owners | Blame, speculation without facts, re-litigating decisions |
| Postmortem (single case deep dive) | Learn (Diagnose/Build) | 45 to 90 min | One event/injury/incident deep review (blameless) | Findings, changes to SOPs, review date | When emotions are high without facilitation; when data is not ready |
| Education meeting (staff-run) | Any (training focus) | 15 to 30 min | Leadership reps for staff; structured practice | Same as chosen modality + brief debrief | Unstructured, unclear purpose, no guardrails |

### 4. Kaigi decision meeting: agenda structure (3A blog pp.1 to 3; 3B blog p.1)

Prerequisites (non-negotiables):

1. A clear question. If vague, it belongs in Diagnose or Build.
2. Limited options, usually 2 to 3. Six options is uncertainty, which is Diagnose.
3. Pre-read when possible: send the information, include the analysis, be explicit about what is known and unknown. "If people arrive cold, you're not deciding, you're catching up."
4. Time-boxing: 120 seconds typical; 30 seconds per point pre-training. If it cannot land quickly, take it offline.
5. Strict outputs in a decision log: Owner, Action, Due date, Review process, recorded as an audit trail.

Agenda template to run it (assembled from the prerequisites and cheat sheet):

- Invite header: "DECIDE (Kaigi). Question: [one sentence]. Options: A / B / C. Pre-read attached; arrive informed. 15 to 30 min."
- Item 1 (2 min): restate the question and the options; state what is known and unknown.
- Items 2 to n (120 s each): each relevant practitioner makes their point. No new information beyond the pre-read.
- Decision (2 min): meeting lead or discipline lead selects the option.
- Log (2 min): owner, action, due date, review method and date, entered in the decision log before anyone leaves.
- Anything incomplete or speculative goes offline or to a Diagnose meeting.

What Kaigi is not for: education sessions, ideation workshops, design studios, or complex work when the information is not ready. "Kaigi is a decision engine, and decision engines only run cleanly on prepared fuel" (blog p.3).

### 5. Pre-training go/no-go Kaigi (3A blog p.2 for the compressed structure; run order is transcript-only, 07:28 to 12:13)

PDF-confirmed structure: multiple feeds arrive quickly (performance monitoring data, testing information, Athletic Medicine input and manual assessment, sometimes coaching constraints). Bring the information, make the point, decide, log it, move. Anything incomplete or speculative goes offline. Cheat sheet time box 5 to 12 min.

Run order as described in the video (AFL example, 50 players, 15 to 17 staff standing, target under 30 seconds per player):

1. Leader reads the first athlete's name. The name is itself the question. If a data flag exists (for example a low readiness score), the leader states it.
2. If the leader says nothing within about two seconds, the responsible pair (the athlete's Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance practitioners) speak: "I've seen this, this, and this."
3. Anyone else on staff who observed something (warm-up, movement, mood, speech) adds it without being prompted. Evidence is stacked; nobody is pulled from training on one signal.
4. If nothing is flagged, silence is the answer and the meeting moves to the next name. Negative space is information.
5. Flagged athletes are batched and assigned on the spot: "One, two, three: head physio, go. Mental health concern: psych, go." Owners leave the room immediately.
6. Owners report back to the leader within 20 minutes so the leader can give the head coach a preliminary clearance ("we're good, four under review, 20 minutes").

The layered web of observers is deliberate: a single sieve lets information through; multiple layers catch it.

### 6. Diagnose to Kaigi mode switch (3A blog p.2; 3B blog p.2; transcript 12:14 to 13:23)

When a problem-solving meeting stalls because perspectives collide, declare the switch out loud: "We're moving from Diagnose to Kaigi for the last 10 to 15 minutes." The job is no longer to explore. Assign responsibility (often the discipline lead), select the option, record it, move forward. If information is genuinely missing, instead assign a small group to gather it inside a defined window and schedule the Kaigi.

### 7. Stoplight Storytelling slide template (template pp.1 to 2, field by field; 3C blog pp.1 to 2)

One slide, two minutes, one ask. Fill every field:

1. Slide title (headline question). DECISION GATE: "What do we need to decide today?" Example: "Change speed exposure dose for Group A this week?"
2. STOPLIGHT STATUS (pick one, with one line why):
   - GREEN (Go / Continue)
   - AMBER (Hold / Monitor / Conditional)
   - RED (Stop / Change now)
3. THE DATA (one chart max):
   - Metric(s): single metric name + unit
   - Window: dates / sessions
   - Baseline: value
   - Current: value
   - Change (delta): value
   - Signal vs noise guardrails: SEM (value + unit); MDC95 (value + unit); Interpretation: delta is below / near / above MDC95, therefore likely noise / uncertain / likely real
4. CHART PLACEHOLDER: one clear chart, axes labelled, difference labelled, readable on-site.
5. CONVERGENT EVIDENCE (max 2 bullets).
6. THE ASK (one ask only, written as a verb): Start / Stop / Change / Limit / Continue + exact action. (The blog p.1 lists four verbs; the template and the 3D worksheet list five, adding Continue.)
7. RECOMMENDED DECISION (one line): "Do X now / Hold until Y / Stop X and replace with Z."
8. ACCOUNTABILITY (must be completed): Owner (name/role); Action (single statement); Due (date/time); Review (date/time + what will be checked).
9. Footer: "2 minutes total. If it needs explaining, it's the wrong meeting type."

Do's: short and sharp, confidence tied to SEM and MDC, clear labelled charts, common language with technical terms stripped out. Don'ts: multiple charts, multiple asks, brand-new information, pretty-but-useless visuals, dual y-axes, anything left hanging. Amber must carry what is monitored, who owns it, and a review date such as 48 hours. If it needs more than one chart, more than one ask, or more than two minutes, it is a Diagnose or Build meeting.

Throughput claim (transcript 07:25 to 07:38): five staff presenting at two to five minutes each clears five decisions in under 30 minutes.

### 8. Decision log (template p.2, copied exactly; cheat sheet p.1 minimum fields)

Row format:

- Date/Time
- Meeting Type (Kaigi / Pre-training Kaigi / Ops / AAR / etc.)
- Decision Gate / Topic
- Stoplight (Green / Amber / Red)
- Ask (verb) (Start / Stop / Change / Limit / Continue)
- Decision (what we decided)
- Rationale (1 to 2 lines)
- Key Data (metric, baseline, current, delta)
- SEM
- MDC95
- Signal vs Noise Call (Noise / Unclear / Real)
- Convergent Evidence (max 2)
- Owner
- Actions (single action)
- Due Date/Time
- Review Date/Time
- Review Method (what will be checked)
- Status (Open / In progress / Done / Superseded)
- Link to slide / file (optional)

CSV header to paste into Sheets (verbatim from template p.2):

```
DateTime,MeetingType,Topic,Stoplight,AskVerb,Decision,Rationale,Metric,Baseline,Current,Delta,SEM,MDC95,SignalNoise,ConvergentEvidence1,ConvergentEvidence2,Owner,Action,DueDateTime,ReviewDateTime,ReviewMethod,Status,Link
```

### 9. Five operating practices for controlling time (Webinar Parts II and III; transcript-only)

1. Common language. Demystify. Report in the coach's verbal anchors, not units. Explain what, why, and how in simple terms and document it in a procedures manual. Brief the media department on what is and is not allowed around athletes. Give coaches a cheat sheet for monitoring and testing before the season; never add a variable mid-season. Ask each coach how they like to receive information and mirror it.
2. Communication mechanisms. State which channel carries which information. Pre-agree the injury-communication tempo with the head coach: athlete made safe first, best estimate after the post-game talk, physician update after next-morning imaging. Deliver post-training reports in the coach's preferred form and volume. Tag messages urgent / routine / FYI. Every meeting invite carries objective, duration, and required prep. Every project assignment carries deliverable, deadline, quality standard, and who to consult. Set expected response times.
3. Operational procedures. Specify exactly how and by whom repeatable tasks are done: equipment service and cleaning, session prep, data collection, testing, lines of responsibility for every piece of equipment. Work on the business, not in it. Procedures can be improved, but staff must review and fix rather than complain in the background. Vague requests ("can we catch up?") trigger anxiety; always say what it is about.
4. Lead by strategic intent. Strategy is the six-lane highway from A to B; tactics is the car changing lanes. Scale lanes to experience (one or two for a first-year hire, six for a trusted ten-year colleague). Make explicit what each person can decide and what must be pushed up. Micromanagement is where leaders lose control of time.
5. Clear and honest feedback. Structured cycle (monthly, half-year). Do not let small things fester. Be direct without demeaning. Document performance conversations. Ask for feedback on yourself.

### 10. Twenty-minute meeting structure and add-ons (Podcast 3; transcript-only)

- Send pre-read 24 hours ahead; it must be read before arrival (also PDF-confirmed at worksheet p.2 Part B: "Request pre-read if needed (24h where possible)").
- Open by stating the required outcome: "This is what has to happen by the end of this meeting."
- Frame the discussion: what is working, what is not, what needs to change.
- Name the arbiter if a decision is required; the leader reads the room's lean and, if in principle agreement, goes with it.
- Close with decision, actions, owners, deadlines, and what the leader wants to hear back.
- Start and end on time with a visible clock or stopwatch.
- Parking lot: off-topic but valuable items get a subject, an owner, and an action, handled by a dedicated process.
- Agile stand-up: 15 minutes daily, three questions (what did I do, what will I do, what is blocking me).
- Two-pizza teams: when a problem is "too complex for 20 minutes", split it into pieces and send a four-to-six person multidisciplinary group (the example is an Athletic Performance coach, an Athletic Medicine practitioner, a logistics staffer, and a dietitian) to report back next week. Four coaches from one discipline in a room produce the same idea.

### 11. Leader techniques inside meetings (3D blog p.2; transcript 06:14 to 08:49)

- Pose the problem, then sit quietly until someone starts. Warning from the blog: this makes some people uncomfortable.
- Assign a staff member in advance to argue the opposite case with data, even a position they do not hold, so the leader can test their own bias against a real argument before deciding.
- Track who speaks and who does not; give quiet staff notice that they will be called on and what to bring.

## Deliverables / exercises

### Lab 3D Worksheet (Lab_3D_Worksheet.pdf, 3 pp.), the module's only formal worksheet

Part A, Senior staff worksheet:

1. Why are we using meetings for development? Tick: build confidence speaking in groups; improve clarity and brevity under time pressure; develop decision-making and accountability habits; improve meeting discipline (agenda, time-boxing, outputs); identify emerging leaders; other.
2. Choose the meeting "training rep" (low stakes first, select one): Ops / stand-up (10 to 15 min); Info broadcast (10 to 30 min); Problem-solving (Diagnose) meeting (~30 min); Kaigi (Decide) meeting (15 to 30 min); After Action Review (15 to 30 min); other. Tick the modality. Write the reason this is the right starting rep.
3. Guardrails (strategy vs tactics). Strategic intent ("six-lane highway"): three non-negotiables that must not change. Tactical freedom ("allowed lane changes"): two things they can adjust in the moment.
4. Success criteria (3 to 5 observable behaviours): meeting type named clearly at the start; agenda and time boxes followed; asks were verbs (Start/Stop/Change/Limit/Continue); outputs captured (owner, action, due date, review); meeting ended on time; decision/action log updated; other.
5. Progression ladder: assign the next four reps with dates. Step-up rule: advance only when they hit at least N out of 5 success criteria (N is left blank for the leader to set).
6. Debrief (5 minutes, immediately after): one thing they did well; one thing to tighten next time; one habit to practise before the next rep.

Part B, Young practitioner worksheet:

1. Ask for the rep. Script: "I'd like the opportunity to run a [meeting type] next week. I'll keep it to [time box], name the modality, and capture outputs in the decision/action log. Could I take the lead on [topic]?"
2. Pick the meeting type (Ops / Stand-up, Info Broadcast, Problem-solving, Kaigi, AAR, Build session) and modality; write why it fits.
3. Prepare: name the modality and purpose in the invite; set agenda items and time boxes; request pre-read if needed (24h where possible); define required outputs (decision/action log); decide what is out of scope.
